newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Morocco calls on voters to collect electoral cards.
newsitem.headline: Morocco calls on voters to collect electoral cards.

text.p: More than 13 million Moroccans were asked on Wednesday to collect their voting cards to elect nearly 25,000 members of local councils throughout the country in June.

The official news agency MAP, quoting an Interior Ministry statement, said they should pick up the cards "to enable voters to fulfill their national duty and participate in the communal elections due on June 13, 1997."
The new cards will be "a permanent document" valid for all elections including legislative and referendum polls, it said.
According to a provisional figures released by the ministry more than 50,000 people, including independent candidates, are standing for local elections.

Moderate tolerated Islamists are also expected to take part in these elections, Abdelilah Benkiran, a leading figure of the fundamentalist Tawhid Wal Islah (Unity and Reform) movement, said. Members of his group would stand as "independent" candidates, he said.
Campaigning for the local elections has been set for the period of May 29 to June 12, the ministry said.
Morocco announced earlier that it had set up a national commission to supervise all electoral operations this year.

According to a royal decree (Dahir Royal), the commission is chaired by supreme court president Driss Dahak and includes interior and justice ministers and members of political parties represented in the existing parliament, MAP added.
A dozen political parties are represented in the 333-seat Chamber of Representatives (parliament), including four opposition groups with a total 125 seats.

The local elections are the first of a series which will culminate in parliamentary elections in September, with a new bicameral parliament being inaugurated by King Hassan on the second Friday of October.
Under the new constitution, the Lower House of parliament will be directly elected through universal suffrage.
Local councils will elect around 80 percent of the members of a new Upper House of parliament being set up under constitutional reforms approved last September.
The Upper House will have power to vote a no-confidence motion in the government and could topple it.
